sections.title: Introduction: junction types and when to use each
sections.summary: A junction is the device for linking more than two road ends. 1.7 knows three types (common/default, direct, virtual); 1.8 adds crossing. The chapter gives a decision table mapping real-world situations to types, plus three global rules: junctions never overlap, direct junctions never carry @connectingRoad, default/virtual junctions never carry @linkedRoad.
concepts: Common junction (type='default'): drivable lanes of different paths may overlap; traffic can cross; paths are explicit connecting roads.
Direct junction (type='direct', 1.7+): traffic can change road (split/merge) but never crosses; roads are linked directly via @linkedRoad, no connecting roads.
Virtual junction (type='virtual'): the main road is not cut; side branches attach at an s-range of the main road.
Crossing (type='crossing', 1.8+): two or more roads cross on the same level but traffic cannot change between them (rail level crossing, ped/bike crossing).
1.9 decision criteria: do lanes overlap? does traffic cross? can traffic change road?
Junction = graph node; connecting roads = graph edges inside the node; incoming roads = edges ending at the node.

sections.title: Common junctions
sections.summary: The default junction type: an area where the incoming roads end and explicit connecting roads (road@junction=junction id) represent every path through it; their lanes may overlap. Outgoing roads are never declared; they are implied by connecting roads ending on them, so a two-way road is both incoming and outgoing. Junctions have no predecessor/successor themselves and are only used where a direct road link would be ambiguous.
concepts: Incoming road: has at least one lane leading into the junction; referenced by connection@incomingRoad.
Connecting road: a normal <road> with @junction=<junction id>; one per path (or per group of parallel lanes).
Outgoing road: implicit; a one-way road that only leaves the junction is NOT an incoming road (Figure 77).
Junction area: dashed polygon; incoming roads end on its edge, connecting roads live inside.
Ambiguity criterion: a junction is needed exactly when a road end has 2+ candidate predecessors/successors.

attributes.name: id
attributes.meaning: Junction id (-1 in road@junction means 'not in a junction').

attributes.name: incomingRoad
attributes.meaning: Incoming road id (required for all but virtual).

attributes.name: contactPoint
attributes.meaning: Which end of the connecting road touches the incoming road (start/end).

rules.text: Use a junction only where roads cannot be linked directly, i.e. where a road end would have two or more possible predecessors or successors.
A junction has no predecessor or successor of its own.
A junction may carry its own name.
Do not create a junction where only two roads meet; link them directly (already a 'should' sentence in 1.7 text, id added 1.9).
@mainRoad, @orientation, @sStart, @sEnd appear only on virtual junctions.
laneLink@overlapZone appears only in direct junctions.

use_cases.how: One common junction; 3 incoming roads ending on the junction area; connecting roads for each permitted movement (up to 6 for two-way arms).
One common junction; 4 incoming roads; one connecting road per lane movement (left/straight/right per turn arrows); controllers listed in junction; signals on incoming roads.

sections.title: Incoming roads
sections.summary: An incoming road owns lanes that lead into the junction and is declared only by being named in connection@incomingRoad. Because outgoing roads are not modelled separately, the same road serves both roles. A connecting road may never also be an incoming road.
concepts: Incoming lane direction depends on which end of the road touches the junction: road ending (successor=junction) -> right lanes (RHT) drive in; road starting (predecessor=junction) -> left lanes drive in.
laneLink@from always references a lane of the incoming road.

attributes.name: incomingRoad
attributes.meaning: Id of the incoming road (required except virtual; -1 if none in a virtual junction).

attributes.name: from
attributes.meaning: Lane id on the incoming road.

attributes.name: to
attributes.meaning: Lane id on the connecting road (or linked road in direct junctions).

rules.text: A connecting road must not be used as an incoming road (no chaining of connecting roads through connections).

use_cases.how: Incoming for its inbound lanes (laneLink from=those ids) and implicitly outgoing for its outbound lanes.
Not incoming; only target of connecting-road successors.
Incoming only; no connecting road ends on it.

right: Example: connection id=0 incomingRoad=1 connectingRoad=2 contactPoint=start with laneLink from=-2 to=-1.
wrong: Chaining two connecting roads inside one junction (connecting road used as incomingRoad). Split long paths into one connecting road with several geometries instead.
changes_1_8_1_9: 1.8 marks incomingRoad as optional in the table but required for every non-virtual type in the description.
figures: Refers back to Figure 77/85.

sections.title: Connecting roads and lane links
sections.summary: Connecting roads are ordinary roads (planView, lanes, elevation) whose lanes describe drivable paths across the junction from incoming lanes to outgoing lanes; lanes not linked have no path. Each connecting road has exactly one <connection>, whose <laneLink>s map incoming lanes to connecting-road lanes. Parallel movements may be modelled as one road per lane pair (no lane change in junction) or one multi-lane road (lane change possible). Linked lanes must join smoothly.
concepts: Path = lane of a connecting road; topology = connection.laneLink (incoming->connecting) + connecting road lane predecessor/successor (connecting->incoming/outgoing).
No laneLink for a lane = no traversable path from it.
Multiple connecting roads x single laneLink: no lane change within junction (Figure 79 roads 28, 64).
One connecting road x several laneLinks: lane change allowed (Figure 79 road 61 with two lanes).
A connecting road may have left and right lanes (e.g. two-way path, sidewalks in 1.8 cross path example).
Connecting road lanes DO carry predecessor/successor lane links to incoming/outgoing roads (Table 48), while incoming-road lanes carry no lane link toward the junction.
Left-hand traffic: driving lanes in reference direction are positive ids; Figure 79 connecting roads use lanes 1, 2.

attributes.name: connectingRoad
attributes.meaning: Connecting road id (not in direct junctions).

attributes.name: contactPoint
attributes.meaning: End of the connecting road that touches the incoming road.

attributes.name: fromLayer
attributes.meaning: 1.8+: permanent (default) or temporary lane layer of 'from'.

attributes.name: toLayer
attributes.meaning: 1.8+: permanent (default) or temporary lane layer of 'to'.

attributes.name: overlapZone
attributes.meaning: 1.8+, direct junctions only, default 100: s-length from junction position where traffic of two overlapping lanes shares space.

rules.text: 1.7: each connecting road is represented by exactly one <connection>; it may have as many lanes as needed.
One <connection> per (incomingRoad, connectingRoad) pair, and its laneLinks only cover lanes that lead into the junction.
Option A: several connecting roads with one laneLink each -> no lane change inside the junction.
Option B: one connecting road with several laneLinks -> lane change inside the junction possible.
Linked lanes join smoothly as for road linkage (position, heading, width, elevation continuity; see road linkage chapter / Annex D).
@connectingRoad not used in direct junctions.
Provide <laneLink>; omitting it is deprecated (strongly recommended).
Connecting road reference lines should run in driving direction when the direction is unique.

sections.title: Priorities of connecting roads
sections.summary: <priority high low> states that one connecting road has right of way over another. It is only needed when priority cannot be derived from signs/signals on or before the junction.
concepts: Priority pairs are between connecting roads (1.9 says 'roads'; crossings use it between crossing roads).

attributes.name: high
attributes.meaning: Id of the prioritised (connecting) road. Optional in 1.7, required 1.8+.

rules.text: Use <priority> only if no signals are defined.
Each <priority> has exactly one @high and one @low.

use_cases.case: unsignalised priority road crossing (OSM highway=primary through residential, no stop/give_way nodes)
use_cases.how: Emit <priority high=<through connecting road> low=<side-road connecting road>> pairs for conflicting movements, or better emit give-way/stop signs on the side-road incoming roads.
Main road always has priority implicitly (1.9: unless specified otherwise).
<priority high=rail road low=street>.

right: Prefer signs/signals; add priority elements only when there are none.
wrong: Priority elements contradicting the traffic lights/signs present.
1.8+: priority with missing high or low.
changes_1_8_1_9: 1.8: high/low become required (high_and_low_attr).

sections.title: Direction of connecting roads
sections.summary: A connecting road may run along or against the travel direction; @contactPoint says which. 'start' means the connecting road's s runs in the direction of the laneLink (from incoming into the junction); 'end' means it runs opposite. Reference lines should follow the driving direction when unique.
concepts: contactPoint=start: connecting road begins at the incoming road; laneLink 'to' lanes are then typically right lanes (RHT) / left lanes (LHT).
contactPoint=end: connecting road ends at the incoming road (drawn backwards); traffic uses its opposite-side lanes.
Two-way connecting road (lanes on both sides) appears in two connections, one from each incoming road, with contactPoint start for one and end for the other.

attributes.name: contactPoint
attributes.meaning: start | end of the connecting road at the incoming road.

rules.text: 'start' when the connecting road runs along the laneLink direction.
'end' when it runs against the laneLink direction.
Place connecting-road reference lines in driving direction if driving direction is unique.

use_cases.how: Always build connecting roads from incoming lane end to outgoing lane start -> contactPoint=start everywhere, driving lanes on the traffic-side (negative ids RHT).

right: Generator-built connecting roads in driving direction with contactPoint='start'.
wrong: contactPoint not matching which end of the connecting road actually touches the incoming road (consumers will route through wrong lane sign).
changes_1_8_1_9: None besides rule ids.

sections.title: Cross paths (1.8+)
sections.summary: A <crossPath> describes a pedestrian/bike path that crosses lanes inside a junction and links a walking/biking lane of one road to a walking/biking lane of another (or the same) road. The path itself is a separate road (crossingRoad) belonging to the junction; its elevation is ignored. Start/end lane links give lane ids and s positions on roadAtStart/roadAtEnd.
concepts: Crossing road: ordinary road with @junction=<id>, usually one walking lane, no links.
roadAtStart / roadAtEnd may be connecting roads (sidewalk lanes on connecting roads, Figure 87) or the main road of a virtual junction.
Lane links carry s on the linked road because the crossing attaches mid-road, not at a road end.

attributes.name: crossingRoad
attributes.meaning: Road that geometrically defines the crossing.

attributes.name: roadAtStart
attributes.meaning: Road at the start of the cross path.

attributes.name: roadAtEnd
attributes.meaning: Road at the end of the cross path.

attributes.name: s
attributes.meaning: s on roadAtStart / roadAtEnd where the crossing attaches.

rules.text: A cross path lies inside a common or virtual junction.
Elevation of the crossingRoad is ignored (it follows the surface it crosses).
Start and end of the crossing road reach the lanes named in startLaneLink / endLaneLink.
Start/end points of the crossing road and its lanes lie fully inside the linked lanes.
Only lanes of type walking or biking may be connected.
crossingRoad@junction equals the owning junction id.

use_cases.how: Mid-block: virtual junction with crossPath (12.7.1). At an intersection: crossPath in the common junction. Alternative: crossing junction (12.8).

sections.title: Direct junctions
sections.summary: Direct junctions link one road on one side directly to several roads on the other side (split or merge) without connecting roads, using connection@linkedRoad. They model motorway entries/exits with fewer roads and are only allowed where no traffic crosses; in 1.7 lanes may not overlap at all, in 1.8+ exactly one overlapping lane pair can be described with overlapZone. The junction sits where the headings of main road and ramp coincide.
concepts: Incoming road ends at junction (successor elementType=junction), linked roads start there (predecessor elementType=junction); all roads have junction=-1 (they are not inside the junction).
laneLink from = incoming lane, to = lane on linked road; lanes of road 1 split between road 2 (-1..-3, plus left lane 1) and road 3 (-4 -> -1).
Overlap (1.8): one lane may continue to two roads (repeated from -> exit) or two lanes may feed one lane (repeated to -> entry); overlapZone gives shared-space length.
Direct junction = graph split/merge node without geometry of its own.

attributes.name: contactPoint
attributes.meaning: Contact point on the linked road.

attributes.name: overlapZone
attributes.meaning: 1.8+: length (s from junction position) of shared space of the overlapping lane pair; default 100.

rules.text: Exactly one road on one side is linked to several roads on the other side.
Only for splits or merges; no crossing traffic.
1.7: only for non-overlapping roads; if entry/exit lanes overlap other lanes use a common junction.
@linkedRoad only in direct junctions.
@connectingRoad never in direct junctions.
Linked lanes fit smoothly as for road linkage.
Place the junction where road and ramp/slip lane have identical heading.
Only one pair of laneLinks carries overlapZone (i.e. only one overlapping lane pair per direct junction).
overlapZone covers at least the overlapping area (may be longer).
Only flat entries/exits can currently be modelled with overlapping direct junctions.

sections.title: Virtual junctions
sections.summary: A virtual junction attaches side branches to a main road between sStart and sEnd without cutting the main road's geometry. Connecting roads (road@junction=id) start or end on the main road at sStart/sEnd using road links with elementS/elementDir. It is the recommended model for driveways, parking entries and farm roads; it has no controllers, the main road has priority, and (1.8+) only flat virtual junctions are possible.
concepts: Main road is the incoming road for branches leaving it; the side road (road 99) is incoming for branches entering the main road.
Connecting roads reference the main road mid-way: <predecessor elementType='road' elementId='1' elementS='50' elementDir='+'/> (road-link attributes elementS/elementDir).
orientation '+'/'-'/'none' says for which main-road driving direction the junction matters.
incomingRoad=-1 when no incoming road exists.
The side road ends at the junction like any incoming road (successor elementType=junction).

attributes.name: elementS
attributes.meaning: s on the main road where the connecting road attaches.

attributes.name: elementDir
attributes.meaning: Direction relative to main road s.

rules.text: The main incoming road need not end before the junction area.
Virtual junctions do not replace common junctions or crossings connecting several roads.
Only for branches off the main road; main road has priority (1.9: unless stated otherwise).
No controllers, hence no traffic lights.
@incomingRoad = -1 if there is no incoming road.
Every connecting road starts or ends at sStart or sEnd.
Exactly one sStart and one sEnd per virtual junction.
Connecting roads have the main road's heading at sStart/sEnd.
Linked lanes fit smoothly.
@mainRoad/@sStart/@sEnd/@orientation valid only for virtual junctions.
1.8+: only flat virtual junctions can currently be modelled.

sections.title: Virtual connections (deprecated 1.8) and cross paths in virtual junctions
sections.summary: Virtual connections (connection type='virtual') state purely topological lane-to-lane connectivity between roads in a virtual junction, with no geometry, using <predecessor>/<successor> children with elementS/elementDir. They were deprecated in 1.8. 1.8 adds cross paths inside virtual junctions for mid-block crossings, where the crossing road must stay within the main road's s and t extent.
concepts: Virtual connection = topology only, reference lines unchanged, need not be geometrically correct (e.g. left turn from road 99 into road 1's opposite lanes at s=60 with elementDir='-').
Cross path in virtual junction: crossingRoad bounded by main road extents.

attributes.name: elementS
attributes.meaning: s where connection meets the road.

attributes.name: elementDir
attributes.meaning: Direction relative to that road's s.

rules.text: Virtual connections do not replace geometric road/lane linkage.
Virtual connections only inside virtual junctions.
Crossing road must not exceed the s/t extents of the main road (roadAtStart/roadAtEnd).
Crossing road reaches the lanes given by startLaneLink/endLaneLink.
Only walking/biking lanes.

use_cases.how: 1.7: virtual connections 99->road1 lanes 1,2 at s=60 (dir '-') and road1 lane 1 at s=70 -> 99 lane 1. 1.8+: avoid (deprecated); model real connecting roads or use a common junction.
Virtual junction + crossPath (Figure 94).

Using virtual connections instead of real connecting roads where geometry is known.

sections.title: Crossings (1.8+)
sections.summary: A crossing junction marks where two or more roads cross on the same level but traffic cannot transfer between them. It contains only <roadSection> elements giving, per road, the s-range where crossing traffic can appear, plus a priority telling which road wins. Currently only flat crossings.
concepts: No connections, no connecting roads: the crossing roads are normal roads (junction=-1) that pass through.
Behaves like a virtual junction from the driving perspective.
Exactly one road has high priority (e.g. the railway).
Elevation may be given by CRG surface or elevation grid but only flat crossings are currently modellable.

attributes.name: sStart
attributes.meaning: Start s of the crossing area on that road.

attributes.name: sEnd
attributes.meaning: End s of the crossing area on that road.

rules.text: Crossing junctions contain only <roadSection> elements (plus priority per the example).
Only one of the referenced roads has high priority.
sStart..sEnd cover at least the overlap area of the roads.

use_cases.how: Road 1 (driving) and road 2 (lane type rail) both junction=-1; junction type=crossing with <priority high=2 low=1>, roadSection road 1 s 50..60, roadSection road 2 s 150..160.

use_cases.case: pedestrian / bicycle crossing as separate road (OSM footway=crossing way)
use_cases.how: Crossing junction between the street and the footway road, or crossPath (12.5/12.7.1).

use_cases.case: tram track crossing a street without turning
use_cases.how: Crossing junction (rail has priority).
No junction at all - roads simply pass at different z; crossing type is same-level only.

right: roadSection ranges cover the full overlap of both roads' widths.
Exactly one high-priority road.
wrong: Connections or connecting roads in a crossing junction.
Using a crossing junction for roads at different levels.
Two roads both high priority.
changes_1_8_1_9: New in 1.8 (type crossing, <roadSection>).
figures: 1.9 Figure 96: crossing of road 1 (driving) with road 2 (railroad); each roadSection marks the s-range of the crossing; road 2 has priority.

sections.title: Junction reference line (1.8+)
sections.summary: A junction may own a <planView> holding a single straight line that acts as its reference line (no lanes, no elevation). It anchors the elevation grid and junction-related objects (islands, potholes with CRG). It must be placed so every junction point is reachable by a perpendicular from it and must cross or touch the boundary.
concepts: Gives the junction its own s/t coordinate frame for elevationGrid rows and objects.
Objects (e.g. roadSurface/pothole) can be placed relative to the junction.

formulas.name: point on junction reference line
formulas.vars: x0,y0,hdg,s0 from <geometry>; t lateral offset (left positive)
formulas.notes: Standard line geometry + reference-line frame; not printed in the junction section but implied.

rules.text: One <geometry> containing only one <line>.
Every junction point must be reachable by a perpendicular from the line (line must span the junction).
If a boundary exists, the line crosses it or touches it tangentially in at least one point.

use_cases.how: Choose line through junction centroid along the main axis (e.g. PCA of the boundary polygon), long enough to cover the projection of the whole boundary.
Place object relative to the junction reference line.

right: Line spanning the whole junction extent so perpendiculars reach all points.
wrong: Arcs/spirals or multiple geometries.
Short line not covering the junction projection.
changes_1_8_1_9: New in 1.8.
figures: 1.9 Figure 97: junction with its reference line (red arrow) crossing the junction area.

sections.title: Junction boundary (1.8+)
sections.summary: <boundary> describes the closed outline of the whole junction area (including sidewalks) as a counter-clockwise sequence of segments: 'lane' segments follow the outer edge of a lane of a (connecting or helper) road over an s-range, 'joint' segments cut perpendicularly across the end of a road. It defines where the elevation grid applies and, via transitionLength, where heights blend from road to grid. Common junctions only.
concepts: Lane segment: outer edge (seen from junction centre) of boundaryLane on roadId from sStart to sEnd ('begin'/'end' keywords allowed; reversed order = traversed backwards).
Joint segment: perpendicular line across road end (contactPoint), optionally only lanes jointLaneStart..jointLaneEnd.
Gaps not coverable by existing roads are closed by helper roads with junction=<id>, no lanes required, no connections, oriented from the incoming/outgoing road into the junction.
A single road can supply multiple lane segments (road 32 split at s=42 between lanes -2 and -1).

attributes.name: boundaryLane
attributes.meaning: Lane whose outer edge is the boundary.

rules.text: Boundaries only for common junctions (currently).
Segments listed counter-clockwise.
Segments reach the start/end of every road connected to the junction.
Segments form a closed outline.
If existing roads cannot close it, add helper roads (junction=<id>, no lanes/connections needed) for the missing parts.
Boundary encloses all sidewalks and similar lanes.

use_cases.how: Alternate: joint across arm A end, lane segment along outer sidewalk lane of the right-turn connecting road A->B, joint across arm B, ... counter-clockwise.

use_cases.case: arm without a right-turn connecting road (e.g. one-way, Figure 99 gap between roads 60 and 3)
use_cases.how: Add helper road (road 100) with junction id to provide the lane segment (boundaryLane 0 = its reference line).

right: Counter-clockwise closed loop alternating joint/lane segments, each arm crossed by a joint segment.
wrong: Clockwise order, open outline, an arm without a joint segment, boundary on direct/virtual junctions.
changes_1_8_1_9: New in 1.8.
figures: 1.9 Figure 98: UML JunctionBoundary.
1.9 Figure 99: boundary built from lane and joint segments; helper road 100 exists only to supply a lane segment closing the gap between road 60 and road 3.

sections.title: Junction elevation grid (1.8+)
sections.summary: <elevationGrid> gives a coarse square grid of z values laid out along the junction reference line (rows perpendicular to it, spaced gridSpacing, starting at sStart). Inside the boundary it overrides all road-derived elevation; lane heights are added on top; heights are bicubically interpolated, and a cubic blend over transitionLength joins incoming roads smoothly. Common junctions only; not a replacement for OpenCRG.
concepts: Row k is at s = sStart + k*gridSpacing on the junction reference line; centre value at t=0, left values at t = +gridSpacing, +2*gridSpacing ... (inside->outside), right values at t = -gridSpacing ...
Grid must extend by complete squares beyond the boundary in all directions; minimum is 4 points forming a bounding square (constant z = flat plane).
Roads crossing the grid outside the boundary keep their own elevation; inside, grid wins (connecting roads are inside so grid always applies to them).
Lane height (sidewalk kerb) is superimposed on grid z.

attributes.name: sStart
attributes.meaning: s of first row on the junction reference line.

attributes.name: center
attributes.meaning: z on the reference line for this row.

attributes.name: left
attributes.meaning: z values to the left, inside to outside.

attributes.name: right
attributes.meaning: z values to the right, inside to outside.

formulas.name: grid point position
formulas.expr: P(k,j) = refline(s = sStart + k*g) + t*n, t = j*g (j>0 left, j<0 right)
formulas.vars: g = gridSpacing; n = left normal of reference line; k = row index (<elevation> order)
formulas.notes: Inferred from rules (rows perpendicular to the reference line, spacing g); the spec does not print this formula.

formulas.name: edge cubic
formulas.expr: f(x) = d x^3 + c x^2 + b x + a
formulas.vars: fitted along grid lines through neighbouring points
formulas.notes: Used to obtain tangents; c=d=0 if not enough support points (rule polynome_coefficient_values).

formulas.name: bicubic patch
formulas.expr: alpha = A * [[Z, Tt],[Ts, Tst]] * A^T ; z(s,t) = [1 s s^2 s^3] * alpha * [1 t t^2 t^3]^T
formulas.vars: Z = 2x2 corner z values; Ts, Tt, Tst = 2x2 partial derivatives in s, t, st at corners; A = constant 4x4 bicubic Hermite matrix; s,t normalised to [0,1] within the square
formulas.notes: Standard bicubic interpolation (12.11.1). A = [[1,0,0,0],[0,0,1,0],[-3,3,-2,-1],[2,-2,1,1]] in standard form.

formulas.name: transition polygon parameterisation
formulas.expr: A = P0 + k (P1 - P0); B = P3 + k (P2 - P3); P = A + l (B - A); solve fx(k,l)=0, fy(k,l)=0
formulas.vars: P0..P3 corners of the transition quad from the joint segment and adjacent lane segments (transitionLength)

formulas.name: road-to-grid blend
formulas.expr: z_P(l) = a + b l + c l^2 + d l^3; a = zA; b = mA; c = -3 zA + 3 zB - 2 mA - mB; d = 2 zA - 2 zB + mA + mB
formulas.vars: zA, mA: road elevation and slope at the road end (A side); zB, mB: grid z and slope along AB at B; slopes scaled by |AB|; l in [0,1]
formulas.notes: Cubic Hermite. Spec text labels the grid slope mA in one place - typo for mB.

rules.text: Elevation grids currently only for common junctions.
At most one elevation grid per junction.
If a boundary exists, the grid covers the entire enclosed area.
Grid vectors perpendicular to the junction reference line.
Grid valid from boundary entry until exit onto outgoing road; overrides elevation of roads that are part of the junction/boundary.
Ensure smooth transition at entries/exits.
Polynomial c and d are 0 when too few support points.

use_cases.case: sloped junction on a hill (OSM incline / DEM)
use_cases.how: Reference line + boundary + elevationGrid sampled from DEM; transitionLength on joint segments for blending into incoming road elevation.

use_cases.case: flat junction with differing incoming road z (DEM noise)
use_cases.how: Minimal 4-point grid at a common z, or keep connecting road elevations consistent.

right: Grid squares fully cover boundary plus one cell margin; row order along reference line.
wrong: Grid not covering boundary; two grids; grid on direct/virtual junction; expecting it to model high-frequency detail (use CRG).

sections.title: Road surface in junctions (CRG)
sections.summary: Junction elevation can be described with OpenCRG data in <surface><CRG>, which then supersedes all elevation data of the connecting roads and can model complex/overlapping surfaces. In 1.7 the only mode was 'global'; from 1.8 the junction CRG attaches to the junction reference line with the road CRG modes and attributes. For non-flat junctions without need for fine detail the elevation grid is recommended instead.
concepts: CRG supersedes connecting-road elevation inside the junction.
1.8+: attaches to junction <planView>; modes attached/attached0/genuine/global as for roads.

attributes.name: orientation, sStart, sEnd, sOffset, tOffset, hOffset
attributes.meaning: 1.8+ road-CRG attributes, relative to the junction reference line.

rules.text: Junction CRG surfaces use the junction reference line (1.8+).
A <surface> in a junction supersedes all elevation of its connecting roads.

use_cases.how: CRG file; otherwise prefer elevationGrid.

right: Use elevationGrid for coarse slopes, CRG only for measured detail.
wrong: Expecting connecting-road elevation to still apply when a junction CRG surface exists.
changes_1_8_1_9: 1.8: switch from e_junction_surface_CRG_mode (global only) to road CRG modes on the junction reference line.

sections.title: Junction groups (roundabouts, interchanges)
sections.summary: <junctionGroup> aggregates several junctions that are perceived as one node for routing, e.g. the arm junctions of a roundabout. Each member is listed with <junctionReference junction=...>. 1.8 adds group types complexJunction and highwayInterchange.
concepts: Roundabout model (Figure 84): one common junction per arm where the arm meets the ring; ring segments between junctions are ordinary roads; the junctions are grouped.
Group is semantic/routing only; geometry and linkage still live in member junctions and roads.

attributes.name: junction
attributes.meaning: Id of an existing junction (1..* references).

rules.text: Two or more junctions may be grouped to show they belong together (roundabout etc.).

use_cases.how: Split ring at each arm; one common junction per arm containing: ring-in -> ring-out (through), ring-in -> arm-out (exit), arm-in -> ring-out (entry); ring arcs between arms are plain roads (junction=-1); junctionGroup type=roundabout referencing all arm junctions. See UC_2Lane-Roundabout-3Arms.xodr.
Direct junctions at each diverge/merge, grouped as highwayInterchange (1.8).

use_cases.case: dual-carriageway crossroads split into 2-4 junctions (OSM: four intersection nodes)
use_cases.how: Common junctions grouped as complexJunction (1.8).

right: Each roundabout arm junction small and non-overlapping; ring segments as normal roads; group lists all.
wrong: One giant junction for a whole large roundabout with ring segments as connecting roads (allowed but loses ring structure; junction areas must not overlap if split).

sections.title: Controllers for junctions / signal synchronization groups
sections.summary: A junction lists the signal controllers that manage it via <controller id type sequence>; sequence ranks controllers within the junction. In 1.8+ this list is reinterpreted as a signal synchronization group: controllers in one junction whose cycles are synchronised, so setting one group (e.g. via OpenSCENARIO TrafficSignalControllerAction) moves the others to the matching phase.
concepts: Global <controller> (child of <OpenDRIVE>) groups signals via <control signalId type>; junction <controller> references those controllers.
Figure 86: 4 lights, 2 controllers - opposite approaches share a controller (same phase).
Figure 110 (1.9): 20 lights mapped to six signal groups/controllers 42-47; if controller 46 goes green, 44 must go red.
type is application-defined free text.

attributes.name: sequence
attributes.meaning: Priority/order among controllers of this junction.

rules.text: Virtual junctions have no controllers (direct junctions also cannot host lights per the usage table).

Separate controller per turn phase; all listed in the junction (one synchronization group).

wrong: Controllers in virtual junctions; one controller for conflicting approaches.
